A learning tool, a personal exploration

Understand the code you write.

Python Code Depth Lifter

It is easy to write another Python file. The greater challenge is to organise your work, find your way back, and understand the ideas inside it. Depth Lifter is one of the utilities I have built to make that journey more constructive.

Programming is a way of disciplining an idea.

When a thought has to become a sequence of precise instructions, you learn to ask what each word means, what each step changes, and how the parts work together.

01

Why I built Depth Lifter

Making my own Python work easier to revisit

A couple of years ago, I began writing a great deal of Python. I found that creating files was easy, but keeping track of their contents was not. Functions and classes accumulated, useful fragments disappeared into older projects, and returning to my own work could take longer than it should.

So I began developing small utilities to make Python more constructive for me. At its simplest, Depth Lifter can sort the definitions in a Python file and, if I choose, place an index at the top. That alone gives me a more useful map of what I have written.

But this is part of a larger experiment. Eventually, I would like a collection of my favourite, reusable Python demonstrations presented almost like a deck of Monopoly cards — organised, colour-coded, and easy to recognise. Each card could help me rediscover a particularly useful block of code instead of trying to remember which file contains it.

Another utility I made, Browse Chris, belongs to the same wider exploration: finding practical ways to browse, inspect, and understand what I have created.

The invitation

These are tools for exploration, not finished monuments.

I welcome suggestions, changes, and new features. The aim is to discover better ways to understand code and to make useful things from it.

02

What Depth Lifter actually does

From a Python file to a structured view

The utility reads Python source and uses its structure to help you examine it. Reading the file for analysis does not run its Python code. You can open a single file directly, or on supported Windows systems drag Python files onto the application to produce reports.

The working versions offer a choice: keep the Original as a read-only reference, use Sorted to rearrange definitions, use Indexed for a depth-aware index, or examine Sorted Indexed for both.

  • Structure: explore functions, classes, nested definitions and line ranges
  • Vars, Calls, Externals: see variables, called names and imported dependencies
  • About: review statistics, file details and possible cautions
  • HTML Publish: build linked code pages and an index of reports

Save carefully

Inspect first. Save when ready.

Sorting can change the order of definitions, which can change program behaviour. Depth Lifter keeps an Original view for reference, and Save File makes a backup before overwriting the loaded source. Separate save commands create separate files.

03

Why coding and language belong together

A precise instruction begins with a precise idea

An idea expressed in code

def greet(name):
    return "Hello, " + name

message = greet("Ada")

We can describe the same short example in ordinary English: define what the function does, accept a value, produce a result, then use it. Those are logical steps, not only programming words.

Notice the difference between a parameter called name and the argument Ada supplied when the function is called. Precise vocabulary explains a precise distinction.

I do not believe that AI-generated code will remove the value of understanding how to program. The art is not simply producing instructions. It is knowing why those instructions work, which assumptions they depend on, and how the logic fits together.

I see a similar art in English. To help another person understand an idea, we must organise it in a logical order, choose words carefully, and explain relationships. The same need for precise definitions appears in legal writing in countries around the world, often across more than one language.

My hope is that learning to build logical structures in code also gives us practice in forming clearer concepts in our minds. It encourages us to ask: What exactly do I mean? What changes? What remains the same? How can somebody else check this?

Try this in English

Explain a small program without using code.

First, the function receives a name. Next, it combines the greeting with that name. Finally, it returns the completed sentence.

Words such as first, next, because, if, and therefore show the links between ideas.

04

How one key can change everything

Computer actions depend on the situation

Here is an ordinary but powerful example. You drag a file from one folder to another. Are you moving it, copying it, or creating a link? The answer depends on the program you are using, where the two folders are, and whether you hold a modifier key.

In Windows File Explorer, dragging to another folder on the same drive normally moves the file. Dragging between different drives normally makes a copy. Holding Ctrl while dragging usually requests a copy, while holding Shift requests a move. A network location may behave according to how it is represented and accessed, so look at the drag indicator before releasing.

This is why a command cannot be understood in isolation. The context changes its meaning. Even a single key can change the result.

Think like a programmer

What conditions determine the action?

Identify the source location, the destination location, the active application, and the key being held. Predict the result before completing the operation.

A simple computer model

Input. Rules. Result.

01 · Input

You act

A click, drag, key press, command or file selection provides information

02 · Context

The system checks

Which app is active, what is selected, and where the data resides

03 · Rule

A choice is made

Software combines your action with its rules and any modifier keys

04 · Result

The state changes

A file may be copied, moved or linked, according to the instruction

Language changes with context too.

The word run means one thing in run a program and something else in run to the station. The surrounding words establish the intended action. AI can also overlook an important situational detail, which is why checking assumptions remains essential.

File handling in Windows File Explorer — common drag-and-drop outcomes
RefWhat you doUsual resultWhat changes the meaning
01Drag a file to another folder on the same driveMoveSource and destination are on the same drive
02Drag a file to a folder on a different driveCopySource and destination are on different drives
03Hold Ctrl while draggingCopyCtrl modifies the normal drag action
04Hold Shift while draggingMoveShift modifies the normal drag action
05Hold Ctrl and Shift while draggingCreate a shortcut where supportedBoth modifier keys change the requested action
06Use Ctrl+C then Ctrl+VCopy and pasteThe explicit copy command does not depend on the drag default
07Drag between a network share and a local folderOften a copy when they are distinct locationsShare mapping, permissions and the software involved can matter
Learning note:

These are typical Windows File Explorer behaviours, not universal rules for every operating system or application. Right-dragging a file normally gives a menu of possible actions. For anything important, verify whether the file remains in its original location.

A little learning routine

Look, identify, explain, test

Reading code and learning English can strengthen each other. A word becomes more useful when you can describe what it does and explain why.

1

Look closely

Open a small Python file and locate one function. Observe its name, arguments, indentation and return value.

2

Identify the words

Use the dictionary below to distinguish definitions, calls, parameters, imports and references.

3

Explain the logic

Describe each step in a complete sentence. Say why it must happen before or after another step.

4

Test the context

Change one value or condition in a safe working copy. Predict and check what changes.

A computing and ESOL word garden

Useful words for understanding code

Short definitions, examples and reasons to learn each term. Search for a word, or choose one from the alphabetical index.

37 words to explore

algorithmargumentarrayast — abstract syntax treebackupblock of datacallclasscode blockcopydecoratordefinitiondictionarydirectory / folderfile pathfunctionimportindentationindexjsonlistmethodmodulemovenesting / depthobjectparameterreferencerelative pathreturn valuescopeshortcutsource codesymbolic linksyntaxvariableworking copy
REF 01

algorithm

noun

A sequence of steps used to solve a problem or complete a task.

Example: A sorting algorithm can arrange function names alphabetically.

Why it matters: The steps matter as much as the answer.

REF 02

argument

noun

A value supplied to a function when it is called.

Example: In greet(name), the value supplied for name is an argument.

Why it matters: An argument is the actual input, not the placeholder in the definition.

REF 03

array

noun

An indexed collection of values, often stored with a consistent data type.

Example: An array might hold thousands of measurements.

Why it matters: Arrays and Python lists have overlapping uses but are not identical.

REF 04

ast — abstract syntax tree

noun

A tree-shaped representation of the structure of source code.

Example: Depth Lifter uses a Python AST to locate definitions and nesting.

Why it matters: A structural tree helps inspect code without running it.

REF 05

backup

noun

A separate saved copy that can help restore earlier contents.

Example: Depth Lifter backs up a loaded file before Save File replaces it.

Why it matters: A working copy alone is not a reliable backup.

REF 06

block of data

noun

A group of values or bytes handled as a unit.

Example: A file can be read as blocks rather than one byte at a time.

Why it matters: Thinking in blocks helps explain how programs group information.

REF 07

call

noun / verb

An instruction that asks a function or method to run.

Example: report() calls a function named report.

Why it matters: A definition describes an action; a call asks for it to happen.

REF 08

class

noun

A blueprint for creating objects with related data and behaviour.

Example: class Report: can define a kind of report object.

Why it matters: Classes organise related attributes and methods.

REF 09

code block

noun

A related group of instructions treated as one unit.

Example: The indented lines after if form a code block.

Why it matters: Grouping instructions makes their shared purpose clearer.

REF 10

copy

verb / noun

To make another instance of data or a file while retaining the original.

Example: Holding Ctrl while dragging in Windows File Explorer normally requests a copy.

Why it matters: A copy preserves the source, unlike a move.

REF 11

decorator

noun

Python syntax that modifies or wraps a function or class definition.

Example: A line beginning with @ can apply a decorator to a function.

Why it matters: Decorators can alter behaviour without rewriting the main function body.

REF 12

definition

noun

The code that declares what a function, class or other named item is.

Example: def total(): begins a function definition.

Why it matters: Defining a function does not usually execute its body.

REF 13

dictionary

noun

A Python mapping that associates keys with values.

Example: settings = {"theme": "light"} pairs a key with a value.

Why it matters: Dictionaries make it easier to retrieve values by a meaningful key.

REF 14

directory / folder

noun

A named location used to organise files and other folders.

Example: The Reports directory can contain an index.html file.

Why it matters: Folders help impose a structure on many related files.

REF 15

file path

noun

An address describing where a file or folder is located.

Example: A path can point to Reports/index.html.

Why it matters: Paths let software find files rather than rely on memory.

REF 16

function

noun

A named reusable group of instructions that can accept inputs and return a result.

Example: def calculate_total(items): defines a function.

Why it matters: A good function has a purpose that can be explained clearly.

REF 17

import

noun / verb

A Python statement that makes names from another module available.

Example: import pathlib loads the pathlib module for use.

Why it matters: Imports show which other modules code depends on.

REF 18

indentation

noun

The spaces at the beginning of a line that indicate code structure in Python.

Example: The body of a Python function is indented.

Why it matters: Indentation is part of the syntax, not merely decoration.

REF 19

index

noun

An organised guide to items and where they can be found.

Example: A Depth Lifter index lists definitions and line numbers.

Why it matters: An index reduces the time needed to revisit your code.

REF 20

json

noun

A text format for exchanging structured data using objects, arrays and values.

Example: An index saved as JSON can be read by another program.

Why it matters: A standard format helps separate programs share information.

REF 21

list

noun

A Python ordered, changeable collection of items.

Example: names = ["Ada", "Grace"] stores two text values.

Why it matters: A list keeps related items together in a defined order.

REF 22

method

noun

A function associated with a class or object.

Example: A Report object might have a save method.

Why it matters: The word method signals a function used in an object context.

REF 23

module

noun

A Python file or module object containing definitions and statements.

Example: An app.py file can act as a module.

Why it matters: Modules let a large project be divided into manageable parts.

REF 24

move

verb

To change the location of an existing file rather than create another independent copy.

Example: Dragging within the same drive in Windows File Explorer normally moves a file.

Why it matters: The destination changes while a separate original is not kept.

REF 25

nesting / depth

noun

The arrangement of structures inside other structures.

Example: A method is nested inside its class in a structure view.

Why it matters: Depth gives a picture of how code fits together.

REF 26

object

noun

An instance of a class that contains data and can have methods.

Example: my_report could be an object created from Report.

Why it matters: Objects combine the information and actions that belong together.

REF 27

parameter

noun

A named placeholder for a value a function expects.

Example: In def greet(name): the name is a parameter.

Why it matters: Parameters describe what inputs a function is prepared to accept.

REF 28

reference

noun

A name, link or other means of identifying or accessing an item.

Example: A variable can refer to an object; an index entry refers to a location.

Why it matters: A reference points to something but is not necessarily a separate copy.

REF 29

relative path

noun

A file location described from another folder rather than from a drive root.

Example: ./Reports/index.html is relative to the current page location.

Why it matters: Relative links can survive when a whole folder moves together.

REF 30

return value

noun

A result sent back by a function using return.

Example: return total sends the value of total to the caller.

Why it matters: A returned value allows one part of a program to feed another.

REF 31

scope

noun

The region of a program in which a name is available.

Example: A local variable inside a function normally has local scope.

Why it matters: Scope limits which parts of code can use a particular name.

REF 32

shortcut

noun

A link that opens another file, folder or program rather than duplicating its contents.

Example: A desktop shortcut can open a Python project folder.

Why it matters: A shortcut is a route to something, not the actual target.

REF 33

source code

noun

The human-readable instructions written by a programmer.

Example: Depth Lifter reads Python source code without running it.

Why it matters: Studying source reveals how a program is constructed.

REF 34

symbolic link

noun

A file-system entry that points to another file or directory path.

Example: A symbolic link can make the same folder accessible from another location.

Why it matters: Deleting or changing the target may leave the link unable to find it.

REF 35

syntax

noun

The rules that determine which code constructions are valid.

Example: A missing colon can cause a Python syntax error.

Why it matters: Precise syntax lets the interpreter recognise your intentions.

REF 36

variable

noun

A name bound to a value or object.

Example: count = 3 binds the name count to an integer value.

Why it matters: Names help people track information as it changes.

REF 37

working copy

noun

An editable version kept separate from the original source.

Example: Depth Lifter offers Sorted and Indexed working copies.

Why it matters: A working copy allows inspection and experimentation before saving.
